processes.description: Staff pass market information to traders and originators: a daily Western pre-scheduled firm electricity price report forwarded by an assistant, weather comparison spreadsheets, press articles on Enron's market role, analyst call notes, and regional supply and market analyses. Some rounds also ask recipients to review circulated data and pull out what is relevant to them, or offer a feed to a colleague who may want it.
steps: A report, article, analysis or set of call notes becomes available or is prepared.
The sender compiles or attaches the material, adding a short note on why it matters.
The material is forwarded to the trading or origination group or to named colleagues.
Recipients read it and, where asked, review it and pull the data relevant to their own work.
Ongoing analyses are assigned to a named person to keep compiling and updating.

automation.approach: Replace the manual daily forwarding of the published price report with a scheduled distribution that posts the report to a shared location and mails a subscribed list, and keep a simple subscription list so people can opt in to feeds instead of being asked one by one.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are the same report forwarded by hand each day, which a scheduled distribution handles well. A short checklist for the sender (which reports go to whom, where they are saved, who maintains each recurring analysis) keeps the remaining manual circulation consistent.

work_estimate.rationale: Most rounds are a forwarded daily price report needing only a minute or two to locate and attach. Fewer rounds involve real preparation: building a hot-days comparison spreadsheet, writing up analyst call notes, or reviewing a shared data set. The mid reflects a mix weighted toward simple forwards; the high covers rounds where a spreadsheet or notes are prepared.

processes.description: Colleagues and outside customers ask for specific price data, such as historical market data for past years ahead of a meeting or a monthly point price at a pipeline location. The person asked looks the figure up in the price sources, waits when a source such as Gas Daily has not been loaded yet, and replies with the price or a data file and an offer to answer questions.
steps: A colleague or customer emails asking for index, point or historical price data for given periods.
The recipient checks which source holds the data and whether it has been loaded.
If the data is not yet available, the recipient checks back later.
The recipient extracts the prices and assembles them in a reply or attachment.
The reply is sent with an offer to answer follow-up questions.

stalls.summary: Requests wait on the price source itself: Gas Daily data was not loaded yet, so the person handling the request had to keep checking back before replying.

automation.approach: Give requesters self-service access to a standard price lookup or a regularly refreshed price extract covering index, basis, Gas Daily and point prices by month, so routine requests are answered without a manual lookup, and flag when a source has not loaded yet.
automation.rationale: The requests ask for the same kinds of figures in the same shape. A standard price-data layout lets the person asked fill or forward it quickly, and lets customers see exactly which points and periods are available.

work_estimate.rationale: A single monthly point price takes a few minutes to look up; a request for historical data across past years needs pulling and arranging a larger set, and waiting on unloaded Gas Daily data adds a recheck. The mid sits between a single figure and a multi-year extract.

processes.description: Desk heads, schedulers and risk staff ask IT or system administrators to add, change or remove users in trading and operations systems such as Sitara, Enpower, RiskTrac, EnronOnline, schedule tools and distribution lists, or to issue trader IDs and passwords. Requests list names and NT usernames; administrators collect access criteria and lists of who should have access per desk, process the request, and confirm by email or automated notice. Around the new company launch, whole desks were set up and verified at once.
steps: A manager or user emails a request naming the people, the system and the access or role needed.
Administrators collect access criteria or a list of who should have access for each region or desk.
The request is entered into the access request system, which notifies approvers.
The administrator creates, changes or removes the accounts, IDs or passwords.
Confirmation goes back to the requester, often with login details or setup instructions.
The requester or desk checks that users can log in and trade, and reports any accounts that failed to set up.

stalls.summary: Administrators wait on desks for the lists of who needs access, and send reminders when responses do not arrive.
Access depends on outside parties sending credentials: the desk waited on new CAISO cards and passwords well after they were expected.
Requests reach the wrong person, such as security badge requests sent to a Portland desk head with the same name, or messages whose destination was unclear.
System migrations failed to carry user accounts over, leaving users unable to work until IT fixed them.

contradictions.summary: IT reported confirming that all traders were set up and ready to trade at go-live, while the desk then found accounts had not been migrated over the weekend.

automation.approach: Route every access request through one form that captures person, username, system, role and approver, keep a per-desk roster of who should have which access so administrators do not have to ask for lists each time, and run a post-migration check comparing the roster with accounts actually set up.
automation.rationale: Requests arrive as free-text emails with names and usernames, and administrators repeatedly ask desks for access lists. A standard request and roster template removes the back-and-forth and gives a list to verify against after system changes.

work_estimate.rationale: Most rounds add or remove one or a few users: gathering names and usernames and entering the request takes a few minutes. Some rounds compile desk-wide lists of traders for IDs or access, or verify setup after a migration, which takes much longer. The mid weights toward single-user changes.
